(p-257) Surah al-Jumu'ah (The Congregation)

It is entirely Medinan, by the consensus of the scholars.

Its opening has already been explained. Abu al-Darda', Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, 'Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, and al-Walid, from Ya'qub, read ﴿al-Malik al-Quddus al-'Aziz al-Hakim﴾ with the nominative (raf') in all of them.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of mentioning the glorification (tasbih) again at the beginning of this surah?

The answer: it is for opening the surahs with the exaltation of God, mighty and majestic, just as they are opened with ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾. When the meaning of the exaltation of God is great, it is good to open with it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who sent among the unlettered (al-ummiyyin) a messenger from among them﴾. He means the Arabs, who did not write. We have explained this meaning in [al-Baqarah: 78]. ﴿A messenger﴾ means Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿From among them﴾ means from their kind and their lineage.

(p-258) If it is asked: what is the point of the favour in his being sent as an unlettered prophet?

On this there are three answers.

The first: to agree with what the prophets before him had foretold of him in their books.

The second: because his condition resembles their condition, so that he would be closer to them in agreement.

The third: lest it be supposed that he knew the books of those before him. What follows this is in [al-Baqarah: 129], up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed they had been before in clear error﴾, that is, before his mission they were only in ﴿clear error﴾, evident, which is polytheism.

(p-259) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And others among them﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

One: He sent Muhammad to others among them, that is, among the unlettered.

The second: He teaches others among them and purifies them. Regarding who the "others" are, there are four views.

The first: they are the non-Arabs (ajam). This was said by Ibn 'Umar and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is the narration of Layth from Mujahid. According to this view, He said "among them" because when they embrace Islam they become of them, since the Muslims are one hand and one community.

The second: they are the Successors (tabi'un). This was said by 'Ikrimah and Muqatil.

The third: all who enter Islam until the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and it is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

(p-260) The fourth: they are the children, related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who have not yet joined them﴾, that is, they have not yet joined them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the bounty of God﴾, meaning Islam and guidance, ﴿and God is the possessor of great bounty﴾ by sending Muhammad (ﷺ).

Then He struck a parable for the Jews who abandoned acting upon the Torah, so the Exalted said: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah﴾, meaning, were charged with acting upon what is in it, ﴿then did not bear it﴾, meaning, did not act in accordance with its requirements and did not fulfil its right, ﴿is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾. Asfar (books) is the plural of sifr, and the sifr is the book. He likened them to a donkey that does not understand what it carries, since they did not benefit from what is in the Torah, which points to belief in Muhammad. [This parable applies to whoever does not act upon the Qur'an and does not understand its meanings. ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people﴾: He condemned their likeness, and what is meant is condemnation of them. The Jews denied the Qur'an and the Torah when they did not believe in Muhammad.] ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, who wrong themselves by denying the prophets.

(p-261) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you claim that you are friends of Allah﴾. This is because the Jews said: "We are the children of Israel, the son of Allah's sacrificed one, the son of Allah's friend (Khalil Allah), and we are closer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than the rest of mankind, and prophethood can only be among us." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Say" to them: If you are friends of Allah, then wish for death, for death is better for the friends of Allah than this world. We have already explained this and what follows it in [al-Baqarah: 94], up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee﴾. This is because the Jews knew that they had ruined the matter of the Hereafter for themselves by denying Muhammad, and they used to hate death. So it was said to them: there is no escape from its descent upon you, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for indeed it will meet you﴾. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs insert the fa' (fa) into every predicate whose subject is one of the relative forms that take a clause, such as "man" (whoever) and "alladhi" (who). So whoever inserts the fa' here treats "alladhi" as having the sense of a conditional response (al-jaza'). In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "Indeed the death from which you flee will meet you" (without fa'), and this is according to analogy, for you say: "Indeed your brother is standing," and you do not say: "then standing." If you said: "Indeed one who strikes you is then a wrongdoer," it would be permissible, since its interpretation is: "Indeed whoever strikes you is a wrongdoer." Al-Zajjaj said: The insertion of the fa' is permissible only because the sentence carries the meaning of condition and response. It is also possible that the sentence is complete at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from which you flee﴾, as if it were said: If you flee from whatever death it is, whether by killing or otherwise, ﴿then indeed it will meet you﴾, and "fa-innahu" would then be a new sentence after the first statement.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 62, verse 9–10:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the call is made for the prayer﴾. This is the call that is proclaimed when the imam sits upon the pulpit (minbar), and there was no other call in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besides it. "When he (ﷺ) sat upon the minbar, Bilal would call the adhan at the door of the mosque, and it was likewise in the time of Abu Bakr and Umar. Then when the people increased in the time of Uthman, he ordered the adhan to be called at a house of his in the market, called al-Zawra'. And when he sat, he would call the adhan there as well."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for the prayer﴾, i.e., for the time of the prayer. And regarding "al-Jumu'ah" (the Friday) there are three readings (lughat). Pronouncing the jim and the mim with a damma, which is the reading of the majority (al-jumhur). And a damma on the jim with the mim sukun, and with it recited Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu Raja', Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Abi Abla, and al-A'mash. And a damma on the jim with a fatha on the mim, and with it recited Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Nakha'i, and Adi ibn al-Fadl from Abu Amr. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever recites with the sukun on the mim, it is a lightening of al-Jumu'ah because of the heaviness of the two dammas. As for the fatha on the mim, its meaning is "that which gathers the people," just as you say: "a man who is a lu'anah" (one who curses the people much), and "dhuhkah" (one who laughs much).

And concerning the naming of this day as the Day of Jumu'ah there are three opinions.

The first: because Adam was gathered (jumi'a) in it. Salman narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Do you know what al-Jumu'ah is?' I said: No. He said: 'In it your father was gathered,' meaning: the completion of his creation on a day."

The second: because the people gather in it for the prayer.

The third: because the created things are gathered in it, since it is the day on which the creation of things was finished.

And concerning the first one who named it al-Jumu'ah, there are two statements.

One of them: it was Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy who named it thus, and the day of Friday used to be called al-Aruba, as related by Abu Salamah. And it was said: he named it so because the Quraysh gathered in it.

The second: the first to name it so were the Ansar, as related by Ibn Sirin.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾. And concerning this "hastening" there are three opinions.

The first: that it is walking, as said by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mas'ud used to recite it "fam-du" (proceed) and would say: "If I recited 'fas'aw' (hasten), I would run until my cloak fell off." Ata said: it is going and walking to the prayer.

The second: that what is meant by "sa'y" (striving) is action, as said by Ikrimah, al-Qurazi, and al-Dahhak, so the meaning is: act with the aim of proceeding to the remembrance of Allah by devoting yourselves to it, and occupying yourselves with purification and the like.

The third: that it is the intention in the heart, as said by al-Hasan. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is hastening with the intention and diligence.

And concerning what is meant by "dhikr Allah" (the remembrance of Allah) there are two statements.

One of them: that it is the prayer, as said by most of the scholars. The second: the admonition of the imam, as said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and leave off trading﴾, i.e., abandon commerce at that time. And according to us: trading is not permissible at the time of the call, and a sale that takes place is void with respect to the one who is obligated to the obligation of the Friday prayer, and with this said Malik, contrary to most scholars.

Section

The Friday prayer is obligatory upon the one who hears the call from the town (misr), if the caller has a loud voice and the wind is still. Malik set its limit at a farsakh (about three miles), and al-Shafi'i did not set a limit. And from Ahmad concerning the limit there are reports similar to these two. The Friday prayer is obligatory upon the people of the villages. Abu Hanifa said: it is obligatory only upon the people of the cities (amsar). It is permissible for the people of a city to establish the Friday prayer in the open ground near the city, contrary to al-Shafi'i. The Friday prayer is not valid with fewer than forty. And from Ahmad: its minimum is fifty. And from him: its minimum is three. Abu Hanifa said: it is valid with three plus the imam, and the number is a condition of the Friday prayer. Abu Hanifa said in one of the two reports: it is valid for him to deliver the sermon alone. Is the Friday prayer obligatory upon slaves? On this there are two reports from Ahmad. According to us, it is obligatory upon the blind if he finds a guide, contrary to Abu Hanifa. The Friday prayer is not valid with slaves and travelers, contrary to Abu Hanifa. Is the Friday prayer and the two Eids obligatory without the permission of the ruler? On this there are two reports from Ahmad. The Friday prayer is permissible in two places within the town when there is need. Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Yusuf said: it is not permissible except in one place. The establishment of the Friday prayer before midday (zawal) is permissible, contrary to most of them. And if the Eid falls on a Friday, attending it suffices in place of the Friday prayer, and this was said by al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i, contrary to most scholars. For people with excuses, it is recommended to pray the Zuhr in congregation. Abu Hanifa said: it is disliked. It is not permissible to travel on Friday after midday. Abu Hanifa said: it is permissible. Is it permissible to travel after the break of dawn? On this there are two reports from Ahmad. It is reported from Ahmad that it is not permissible to go out on Friday except for jihad. Abu Hanifa said: it is permissible for every journey. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible at all.

The sermon (khutbah) is a condition of the Friday prayer. Dawud said: it is recommended. Purity is not a condition for the sermon, contrary to one of al-Shafi'i's two views. Standing is not a condition for the sermon, contrary to al-Shafi'i. Sitting between the two sermons is not obligatory, contrary to him as well.

Among the conditions of the sermon: praising Allah (tahmid), sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), reciting a verse, and admonition. Abu Hanifa said: it is permissible to deliver the sermon with a single tasbih.

The two sermons are obligatory. As for the recitation in the second sermon, it is a condition, contrary to al-Shafi'i.

The Sunnah for the imam, when he ascends the minbar and faces the people, is that he gives salam, contrary to Abu Hanifa and Malik. Is speaking forbidden while the sermon is being heard? On this there are two reports from Ahmad. It is forbidden for the listener but not for the speaker, contrary to most scholars. Speaking is not disliked before the sermon begins or after it finishes, contrary to Abu Hanifa.

It is recommended for him to pray the greeting of the mosque (tahiyyat al-masjid) while the imam is delivering the sermon, contrary to Abu Hanifa and Malik.

Whether one may deliver the sermon while another leads the prayer: on this there are two reports from Ahmad.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is better for you, if you only knew﴾, i.e., if you have knowledge of what is more beneficial. ﴿And when the prayer is concluded﴾, i.e., when you have finished from it, ﴿disperse in the land﴾: this is a command of permission. ﴿And seek of the bounty of Allah﴾: a permission to seek provision through trade, after the prohibition from it by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and leave off trading﴾. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr said: it is the seeking of knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 62, verse 9–10:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the call is made for the prayer﴾. This is the call that is proclaimed when the imam sits upon the pulpit (minbar), and there was no other call in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besides it. "When he (ﷺ) sat upon the minbar, Bilal would call the adhan at the door of the mosque, and it was likewise in the time of Abu Bakr and Umar. Then when the people increased in the time of Uthman, he ordered the adhan to be called at a house of his in the market, called al-Zawra'. And when he sat, he would call the adhan there as well."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for the prayer﴾, i.e., for the time of the prayer. And regarding "al-Jumu'ah" (the Friday) there are three readings (lughat). Pronouncing the jim and the mim with a damma, which is the reading of the majority (al-jumhur). And a damma on the jim with the mim sukun, and with it recited Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu Raja', Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Abi Abla, and al-A'mash. And a damma on the jim with a fatha on the mim, and with it recited Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Nakha'i, and Adi ibn al-Fadl from Abu Amr. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever recites with the sukun on the mim, it is a lightening of al-Jumu'ah because of the heaviness of the two dammas. As for the fatha on the mim, its meaning is "that which gathers the people," just as you say: "a man who is a lu'anah" (one who curses the people much), and "dhuhkah" (one who laughs much).

And concerning the naming of this day as the Day of Jumu'ah there are three opinions.

The first: because Adam was gathered (jumi'a) in it. Salman narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Do you know what al-Jumu'ah is?' I said: No. He said: 'In it your father was gathered,' meaning: the completion of his creation on a day."

The second: because the people gather in it for the prayer.

The third: because the created things are gathered in it, since it is the day on which the creation of things was finished.

And concerning the first one who named it al-Jumu'ah, there are two statements.

One of them: it was Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy who named it thus, and the day of Friday used to be called al-Aruba, as related by Abu Salamah. And it was said: he named it so because the Quraysh gathered in it.

The second: the first to name it so were the Ansar, as related by Ibn Sirin.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾. And concerning this "hastening" there are three opinions.

The first: that it is walking, as said by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mas'ud used to recite it "fam-du" (proceed) and would say: "If I recited 'fas'aw' (hasten), I would run until my cloak fell off." Ata said: it is going and walking to the prayer.

The second: that what is meant by "sa'y" (striving) is action, as said by Ikrimah, al-Qurazi, and al-Dahhak, so the meaning is: act with the aim of proceeding to the remembrance of Allah by devoting yourselves to it, and occupying yourselves with purification and the like.

The third: that it is the intention in the heart, as said by al-Hasan. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is hastening with the intention and diligence.

And concerning what is meant by "dhikr Allah" (the remembrance of Allah) there are two statements.

One of them: that it is the prayer, as said by most of the scholars. The second: the admonition of the imam, as said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and leave off trading﴾, i.e., abandon commerce at that time. And according to us: trading is not permissible at the time of the call, and a sale that takes place is void with respect to the one who is obligated to the obligation of the Friday prayer, and with this said Malik, contrary to most scholars.

Section

The Friday prayer is obligatory upon the one who hears the call from the town (misr), if the caller has a loud voice and the wind is still. Malik set its limit at a farsakh (about three miles), and al-Shafi'i did not set a limit. And from Ahmad concerning the limit there are reports similar to these two. The Friday prayer is obligatory upon the people of the villages. Abu Hanifa said: it is obligatory only upon the people of the cities (amsar). It is permissible for the people of a city to establish the Friday prayer in the open ground near the city, contrary to al-Shafi'i. The Friday prayer is not valid with fewer than forty. And from Ahmad: its minimum is fifty. And from him: its minimum is three. Abu Hanifa said: it is valid with three plus the imam, and the number is a condition of the Friday prayer. Abu Hanifa said in one of the two reports: it is valid for him to deliver the sermon alone. Is the Friday prayer obligatory upon slaves? On this there are two reports from Ahmad. According to us, it is obligatory upon the blind if he finds a guide, contrary to Abu Hanifa. The Friday prayer is not valid with slaves and travelers, contrary to Abu Hanifa. (p-269) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they see a trade﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was delivering the Friday sermon when a caravan arrived, having come in, so they went out to it, until only twelve men remained with him. Then this verse was revealed." Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it in their two Sahihs from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah. Al-Hasan said: "They had been struck by hunger and high prices, so when they heard of it they went out to it. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If the last of them had followed the first, the valley would have blazed with fire upon them.'" The exegetes said: The one who came with the trade was Dihya ibn Khalifa al-Kalbi. Muqatil said: "That was before he embraced Islam." They said: He came with it from Syria, and a drum was beaten for it to inform the people of its arrival. This was their custom whenever a caravan arrived. Jabir ibn Abdullah said: "The trade was food." Abu Malik said: "It was oil." By "amusement" is meant the beating of the drum. "They dispersed" means: they scattered away from you and went to it. The pronoun refers to the trade. The pronoun was singled out to refer to it because it was more important to them; this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "And when they see a trade (p-270) they disperse toward it, or amusement, they disperse toward it," so the predicate of one of them is omitted, because the second predicate indicates the omitted one. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Abla read "they dispersed toward them both" in the dual. And from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Abla: "they dispersed toward it," with a masculine pronoun. ﴿And they left you standing﴾, and this standing was during the sermon. ﴿Say: What is with Allah﴾ of the reward of prayer and steadfastness with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ﴿is better than amusement and than trade, and Allah is the best of providers﴾, because He provides for those who believe in Him and worship Him and for those who disbelieve in Him and deny Him. He gives to whoever asks, and bestows upon whoever does not ask. Others only provide for those whose benefit they hope for and who devote themselves to serving them.
